author: Emily Dickinson

span.from: Because I could not stop for Death

why: Death as a courteous driver: the most famous opening in American verse.

author: Emily Dickinson
location: Poems, Second Series (1891), “I’m nobody! Who are you?”, lines 1–2

span.from: I’m nobody! Who are you

why: Pure delight, and a comfort to every quiet person.

author: William Shakespeare

span.from: Let me not to the marriage of true minds
span.to: Or bends with the remover to remove

why: The great definition of constant love.

author: William Shakespeare

span.from: All the world’s a stage

speaker: Jaques
why: Life as a play in seven acts: known by everyone.

author: William Shakespeare

span.from: We are such stuff

speaker: Prospero
why: The most beautiful lines Shakespeare wrote about mortality.

author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson

span.from: ’Tis better to have loved and lost
span.to: never to have loved at all

why: The most quoted consolation in English, verified in its section.

author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow

span.from: The heights by great men reached and kept

why: Quiet persistence in four lines.

author: John Keats

span.from: Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness

why: The season in two lines; delight for autumn days.

author: Percy Bysshe Shelley

span.from: We look before and after

why: 'Our sweetest songs…': sorrow and beauty bound together.

author: William Blake
location: The plate after the second “A Memorable Fancy”

span.from: If the doors of perception were cleansed

why: Blake's vision line, as he engraved it.

author: Rudyard Kipling

span.from: If you can keep your head when all about you

why: The opening of If—, verified (it was cut from the starters).

author: Rudyard Kipling

span.from: If you can meet with Triumph and Disaster
span.to: those two impostors just the same

why: Triumph and Disaster as impostors: steadying in any season.

author: Rabindranath Tagore

span.from: Where the mind is without fear

why: Tagore's great prayer for a free mind.

author: Omar Khayyam

span.from: The Moving Finger writes
span.to: wash out a Word of it

why: Time cannot be unwritten: one of the most quoted quatrains in English.

author: Zhuangzi
location: Chapter II, “The Identity of Contraries”, last paragraph

span.from: Once upon a time, I, Chuang
Now I do not know whether I was then a man
span.to: butterfly dreaming I am a man

why: The butterfly dream, delight and philosophy together.

author: Victor Hugo

span.from: The supreme happiness of life consists in the conviction
span.to: loved in spite of one’s self

why: Hugo on being loved in spite of ourselves.

author: Jane Austen
location: Chapter XXIII, Captain Wentworth’s letter to Anne

span.from: You pierce my soul
span.to: such precious feelings are gone for ever

speaker: Captain Wentworth
why: The most famous love letter in English fiction.

author: Jane Austen
location: Chapter XXIII, Anne Elliot to Captain Harville

span.from: All the privilege I claim for my own sex

speaker: Anne
why: Anne's quiet claim: women love longest.

author: Emily Brontë

span.from: Whatever our souls are made of
span.to: his and mine are the same

speaker: Catherine
why: The line that defines Wuthering Heights.

author: Charles Dickens

span.from: Heaven knows we need never be ashamed of our tears

why: Tears as rain on hard hearts: deep consolation.

author: Abraham Lincoln
location: First Inaugural Address, 4 March 1861, closing paragraph

span.from: We are not enemies, but friends

why: Lincoln's plea for friendship across a divide.

author: Abraham Lincoln
location: Address at Cooper Institute, New York, 27 February 1860, closing words

span.from: Let us have faith that right makes might

why: Faith that right makes might: rousing and plain.

author: Theodore Roosevelt

span.from: It is not the critic who counts
span.to: marred by dust and sweat and blood

why: The man in the arena, verified (it was cut from the starters).

author: John Muir

span.from: Climb the mountains and get their good tidings

why: Muir's most loved line: nature's peace flows in.

author: Thomas Paine

span.from: Tyranny, like hell, is not easily conquered

why: The harder the conflict, the more glorious the triumph.

author: G. K. Chesterton

span.from: Angels can fly because they can take themselves lightly

why: Lightness as a virtue: Chesterton's delight.

author: Oscar Wilde

span.from: Where there is sorrow there is holy ground

why: Wilde's prison letter: sorrow made sacred.

author: Herman Melville

span.from: It is not down in any map

why: True places are never on the map.

author: Ella Wheeler Wilcox

span.from: Laugh, and the world laughs with you

why: Wilcox's famous truth about company and sorrow.

author: Julian of Norwich
location: Chapter XXVII, the Thirteenth Revelation, the answer given to Julian

span.from: all shall be well, and all shall be well
span.to: all manner of thing shall be well

why: The great consolation, in Warrack's 1901 rendering.

author: W. B. Yeats
location: “He wishes for the Cloths of Heaven”, last lines

span.from: But I, being poor, have only my dreams

why: Tread softly: the most tender ending in Yeats.

author: Henry David Thoreau

span.from: in Wildness is the preservation of the World

why: Thoreau's line for every wild place.
